items.headline: Google Launches AI Tool to Add Interactivity to E-books
items.excerpt: Google's Expert Intelligence lets readers query e-books bought from the Google Play store, run quizzes, and generate infographics from the text. It launches with more than 100,000 titles, mostly trade nonfiction, from publishers including Penguin Random House, Macmillan and Bloomsbury, with answers restricted to the book itself rather than aggregated model training data.

items.headline: Elsevier Launches AI Assistant for Healthcare E-books
items.excerpt: Elsevier has launched Nora AI, an assistant embedded inside its e-books on VitalSource's Bookshelf platform. Healthcare students and educators can ask questions and get evidence-based answers drawn directly from Elsevier content without leaving the book.

items.headline: Google launches Expert Intelligence with more than 100k publisher titles
items.excerpt: Google has launched Expert Intelligence, letting readers use purchased e-books and other trusted sources directly inside its AI products. UK publishers are among the rights holders supplying the initial catalogue of over 100,000 titles.

items.headline: Who is Narrating the Future? AI and the Audiobook Market
items.excerpt: A new white paper from Frankfurter Buchmesse, produced by Dosdoce.com, maps how quickly the audio industry is adopting AI narration and translation — and where publishers still hold back.

items.headline: U.S. Department of Justice Files Legal Brief Urging Court to Find AI Training to Be Fair Use
items.excerpt: In a 20-page Statement of Interest, DOJ lawyers told the judge in the consolidated authors' case that requiring paid licensing for training data would put U.S. AI companies at a competitive disadvantage — the first time the federal government has taken a side in an AI training copyright suit.

items.headline: Authors push back as publishers and agents make claims on Anthropic settlement
items.excerpt: As payouts from the $1.5 billion Anthropic copyright settlement begin, authors say publishers and agents appear to be claiming more than their contractual share of the roughly $3,000 owed per infringed work.

items.headline: How Good Are AI Custom-Written Novels?
items.excerpt: Ember Novels shows that AI can now develop and carry a plot across 300 pages with fewer continuity errors than many human-written drafts — a test of how far machine-generated long-form fiction has actually come.

items.headline: FTC asked to investigate destruction of books
items.excerpt: More than a dozen groups have asked the Federal Trade Commission to examine the practice of buying, scanning and destroying physical books to build AI training corpora.

items.headline: Authors Guild publishes survey results about copyright registration failures
items.excerpt: Authors ruled ineligible for the Anthropic settlement discovered their publishers never registered their titles with the U.S. Copyright Office — an administrative failure that is now costing writers real money.

items.headline: When Your AI Knows You Too Well: Personalization, Sycophancy, and the Risk of an Intellectual Echo Chamber
items.excerpt: As AI research assistants learn a reader's preferences, they also get better at mirroring that reader's assumptions. The piece argues that avoiding an intellectual echo chamber in research reading will take more than better prompting.

items.headline: The Human Layer: Why AI Makes Academic Libraries More Essential, Not Less
items.excerpt: A guest post arguing that AI's opportunity is not to strip the human layer out of scholarship and library curation, but to make explicit why that layer has always mattered.

items.headline: We Can Now Track AI-generated Content. It Doesn't Solve the Real Problem.
items.excerpt: Provenance signals for AI-generated text are now embedded in Claude models, but the author argues detection alone does not answer the harder editorial question of what AI use is acceptable — and creates new problems of its own.

items.headline: AI Updates, Remembering Dolly Parton, and More News for Library Workers
items.excerpt: Book Riot's weekly roundup for library workers leads with the latest AI developments hitting libraries — from vendor AI features to policy fights over AI-generated material in collections.

items.headline: How Independent Publishers Can Use AI Drawing Lip Sync to Invite Readers Into a Story
items.excerpt: A how-to for indie publishers on using AI lip-sync animation to give original book illustrations a speaking voice as a promotional on-ramp into the full text.
